units.title: Fashion
units.intro: Grammar: the present continuous for actions continuing over a period, confusing verbs (accept/except, adapt/adopt), and the present perfect continuous for actions that started in the past and are still going on.

lessons.title: Present continuous for a period of time

cards.title: Present continuous for a period of time
rule: **am/is/are + -ing** describes actions happening now **or around now**, over a period: *Young people **are wearing** traditional clothes again this year.* It also shows changing trends: *Fashion **is becoming** more expensive.*
State verbs (*know, like, want, belong, understand*) are not normally used in the continuous: *I **like** this dress* (not *am liking*).

examples.text: These days many students are learning to sew.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: I failed the national biology matriculation exam; I ________ harder instead of wasting my time on social media.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The context 'I failed...; I [blank] harder' indicates a past regret or criticism of an action that was advisable but did not happen.
This requires the past regret modal structure (should have + V3).
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Students often confuse 'must have studied' (logical deduction of fact) with 'should have studied' (regret).

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: According to the laboratory safety rules, you ________ enter the chemistry room without wearing safety goggles.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the sentence.** The context describes a strict laboratory safety rule.
This requires a modal of prohibition to show the action is forbidden (must not + V (base)).
**Step 2: Watch out for the trap.** Students often confuse 'don't have to' (lack of obligation/optional) with 'must not' (prohibition/forbidden).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Aster has been studying and living in London for ten years, so she ________ speak English very fluently.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The context presents strong present evidence ('living in London for ten years'). This requires a modal of present logical deduction to show high certainty (must + V (base)).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students sometimes choose 'must have' (Option D), but 'must have' is for past deduction (must have + V3) and cannot be followed by the base verb 'speak'. Option A is correct.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ኣብ ህልው እዋን ዘሎ ናይ ምርግጋጽ ስነ-ሞጎት (present logical deduction) የርእየና። 'ዓሰርተ ዓመት ኣብ ሎንዶን ስለ ዝነበረት' ዝብል መርትዖ ስለ ዘሎ፡ 'ብርግጽ ብጽቡቕ ትዛረብ እያ' ንምባል 'must' (Option A) ክንጥቀም ኣለና። 'must have' ግን ንሕሉፍ እዋን ጥራይ እዩ ዘገልግል።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The soccer field is completely covered in puddles; it ________ heavily during the night.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Look at the sentence**
The present evidence 'The soccer field is completely covered in puddles' leads to a strong positive deduction about a past event. This requires 'must have' (must have + V3).

**Step 2: Watch out for the trap**
Students often confuse 'should have rained' (past regret/unrealized advice) with 'must have rained' (past deduction of fact). Option A is incorrect because we are deducing a fact based on physical evidence, making Option B correct.

**Step 3: In Tigrinya**
'እቲ ናይ ኲዕሶ እግሪ ሜዳ ብማይ ተሸፊኑ ኣሎ' ዝብል ናይ ዓይኒ መርትዖ ስለ ዘለና፡ 'ትማሊ ምሸት ብርግጽ ዓቢ ዝናብ ዘኒቡ ክኸውን ኣለዎ' (past logical deduction) ንምባል 'must have rained' (Option B) ክንመርጽ ኣለና። 'should have' ግን ጣዕሳ ጥራይ እዩ ዝገልጽ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "Why are you walking to school?" "My bicycle is broken, so I ____ this week."
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "this week" and the broken bicycle show a temporary situation.

**Step 2:** Use the present continuous: am walking.

**Step 3:** The present simple would suggest a permanent habit.

**Tip:** Present continuous can describe a temporary situation around now (this week, these days). Watch confusing pairs: lie/lay, rise/raise, borrow/lend, wear/dress.

cards.title: Confusing verbs
rule: **accept** = agree to take (*accept a gift*); **except** = not including (preposition: *everyone **except** me*).
**adapt** = change to suit (*adapt to a new climate*); **adopt** = take as your own (*adopt a new style; adopt a child*).

examples.text: He adapted quickly to city life.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "Everyone came accept Ruth."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** **accept** = agree to take (*accept a gift*); **except** = not including (preposition: *everyone **except** me*).
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "Everyone came accept Ruth." breaks this rule.
**Check:** **adapt** = change to suit (*adapt to a new climate*); **adopt** = take as your own (*adopt a new style; adopt a child*).

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Present continuous (am/is/are + -ing) is for actions in progress now or over a current period and for trends; state verbs stay simple. Accept (verb) vs except (not including); adapt (change to suit) vs adopt (take as your own).

cards.title: Step by step: Confusing verbs
body: **Step 1:** lie – lay – lain (intransitive, no object: rest flat): "I lie down after lunch." lay – laid – laid (transitive, needs an object: put down): "She laid the book on the table."
**Step 2:** rise – rose – risen (no object: go up): "The sun rises." raise – raised – raised (with an object: lift): "Raise your hand."
**Step 3:** sit – sat – sat (no object) vs set – set – set (put something).
**Step 4:** say vs tell: say something (to someone); tell someone something: "He said that…", "He told me that…".
**Step 5:** borrow (take from) vs lend (give to); bring (towards the speaker) vs take (away from the speaker).
**Example:** "Yesterday the price of sugar (raised/rose)." → rose (no object). "Can you (borrow/lend) me your pen?" → lend. "She (said/told) me the answer." → told (there is a person object).

cards.title: Mnemonic — "rAIse, lAY, sET take An object"
body: the verbs with the "a/e" sound before the object are the transitive ones.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Ask "does the verb have an object right after it?" If yes, choose lay / raise / set / tell / lend; if no, choose lie / rise / sit / say.

**Step 3:** "lend" would mean the speaker gives it.

**Tip:** Present continuous can describe a temporary situation around now (this week, these days). Watch confusing pairs: lie/lay, rise/raise, borrow/lend, wear/dress.

**Tip:** Present continuous can describe a temporary situation around now (this week, these days). Watch confusing pairs: lie/lay, rise/raise, borrow/lend, wear/dress.

cards.title: Present perfect continuous: form and use
rule: **Form:** have/has + been + verb-ing. *I **have been waiting**. She **has been studying**.*
**Negative:** have/has + not + been + -ing: *They **haven't been sleeping** well.* **Question:** Have/Has + subject + been + -ing? ***Has** she **been working** here long?*
**Use 1 – it started in the past and is still going on now** (often with *for, since, How long…?*): *I **have been learning** English **for** six years.* *It **has been raining since** 8 o'clock.*
**Use 2 – it has just stopped and we can see the result now:** *Your eyes are red. **Have** you **been crying**?* *I'm hot because I**'ve been running**.*
**for** + a period of time (*for two hours, for a week*); **since** + the starting point (*since Monday, since 2020, since I was ten*).
State verbs (*know, like, believe, own, understand*) do not take -ing: *I **have known** her for years* (not *have been knowing*).

examples.text: She has been sewing dresses since this morning.
We have been waiting for the bus for forty minutes.
I am living in Keren since 2020.
examples.fix: I have been living in Keren since 2020.

examples.text: He has been knowing me for years.
examples.fix: He has known me for years.

examples.text: They have been work all day.
examples.fix: They have been working all day.

cards.title: Timeline: the action continues up to now
body: 8:00 am – Selam starts sewing.  →  11:00 am (now) – she is still sewing.
**Selam has been sewing for three hours.** / **Selam has been sewing since 8 o'clock.**
The line starts in the past and reaches **now**. The present perfect continuous looks at the **whole line** and says **how long** it has lasted.
Compare: *Selam **is sewing**.* (only now) – *Selam **has been sewing** for three hours.* (from 8:00 until now)

cards.title: Present perfect or present perfect continuous?
head: Present perfect (have + V3)
Present perfect continuous (have been + -ing)
rows: the result: how much / how many
I have been writing letters all morning.
Maybe not finished: still going on, or just stopped.
I have known him for years. ✔
She has read the book. (she finished it)
She has been reading the book. (not finished yet)

cards.title: Step by step: present perfect or present perfect continuous?
cards.problem: Complete: (a) Dawit ____ (play) football since 3 o'clock. He is very tired. (b) He ____ (score) two goals. (c) How long ____ you ____ (wait) for me? (d) I ____ (know) Ruth since primary school.

steps.text: **Step 1: Look for the clue words.** (a) *since 3 o'clock* + tired → an activity that has lasted until now. (b) *two goals* → a number = result. (c) *How long* → activity. (d) *know* → a state verb.
**Step 2: Activity + how long → have/has been + -ing.** (a) Dawit **has been playing**. (c) How long **have** you **been waiting**?
**Step 3: Result / number → have/has + V3.** (b) He **has scored** two goals.
**Step 4: State verb → never -ing.** (d) I **have known** Ruth since primary school.

cards.answer: (a) has been playing (b) has scored (c) have … been waiting (d) have known

cards.title: Memory tip
body: **HAVE BEEN + -ING = How long?** Ask *How long?* → have been + -ing. Ask *How many?* → have + V3.
**For** a period (*for 3 hours*), **since** a point (*since 3 o'clock*).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: We ____ for the bus for forty minutes, and it still hasn't come.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *for forty minutes* + *it still hasn't come* → the waiting started in the past and is still going on.

**Step 2:** Use **have been + -ing**: *have been waiting*.

**Step 3:** *are waiting* does not show how long; *had waited* is past perfect.

**Tip:** for/since + still going on → present perfect continuous.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Aster ____ in this laboratory since she finished university five years ago.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *since she finished university* gives the starting point; she still works there.

**Step 2:** Started in the past + still true now → **has been working**.

**Step 3:** *is working* is a common mistake: English does not use the present continuous with *since*.

**Tip:** since + a starting point → have/has (been).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.why:
**Step 1:** We can see a result now (dirty hands) of an activity that has just stopped.

**Step 2:** Use the present perfect continuous: *What have you been doing?*

**Step 3:** *have you done* asks about a finished result, not the activity that made your hands dirty.

**Tip:** A visible result of a recent activity → have been + -ing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I ____ three chapters of the book today.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** *three chapters* is a number – the result.

**Step 2:** Result / how many → present perfect: **have read**.

**Step 3:** *have been read* is a passive form – wrong here.

**Tip:** How many? → have + V3. How long? → have been + -ing.

cards.title: Quick check

options.A: I have been knowing Saba for ten years.
options.B: I know Saba since ten years.
options.C: I have known Saba for ten years.
options.D: I am knowing Saba for ten years.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** *know* is a state verb: no -ing.

**Step 2:** Started in the past and still true → present perfect: *have known*.

**Step 3:** *for* + a period (*ten years*), not *since*.

**Tip:** State verbs (know, like, own, believe) use the present perfect, not the continuous.

glossary.meaning: A verb for a state, not an action (know, like, belong): not used in -ing form.
have/has + been + verb-ing: an action that started in the past and is still going on (or has just stopped).
for + a period (for two hours); since + a starting point (since Monday).

tips.text: acc**E**pt = **E**mbrace it; **EX**cept = **EX**clude it. ad**A**pt = **A**lter; ad**O**pt = **O**wn it.
**How long?** → have been + -ing. **How many?** → have + V3.

Present perfect: **have done**.
questions.tip: Clue words: for / since / How long? / all day → have been + -ing. How many? / a number / finished result → have + V3.

questions.q: They have been building the new school ____ last year.

similar.q: Complete: "I have been waiting ____ two hours."

why: Answer B: since
*last year* is a starting point.
Starting point → **since**.
questions.tip: Clue words: for / since / How long? / all day → have been + -ing. How many? / a number / finished result → have + V3.

questions.q: We ____ (wait) for you for an hour! Where were you?
why: *for an hour* up to now → **have been waiting**.
questions.tip: Clue words: for / since / How long? / all day → have been + -ing. How many? / a number / finished result → have + V3.

questions.q: Selam ____ (sew) traditional dresses since she was fifteen.
why: *since she was fifteen* + still doing it → present perfect continuous.
*Selam* = she → **has** been sewing.
questions.tip: Clue words: for / since / How long? / all day → have been + -ing. How many? / a number / finished result → have + V3.

questions.q: I ____ (know) my best friend since primary school.

similar.q: Complete: "He ____ (own) this shop for ten years."

why: *know* is a state verb: no -ing.
Started in the past and still true → **have known**.
questions.tip: Clue words: for / since / How long? / all day → have been + -ing. How many? / a number / finished result → have + V3.

questions.q: Correct the error: "I am studying English since 2019."

similar.q: Correct: "She is living here for five years."
similar.a: She has been living here for five years.

accept: I have been studying English since 2019
questions.answer: I have been studying English since 2019.
why: *since 2019* → from a past point until now.
Do not use the present continuous with since: **have been studying**.
questions.tip: Clue words: for / since / How long? / all day → have been + -ing. How many? / a number / finished result → have + V3.

questions.q: Make a question with "How long": "They have been playing football." (How long…?)

similar.q: Make a question: "She has been crying." (How long…?)
similar.a: How long has she been crying?

accept: How long have they been playing football
questions.answer: How long have they been playing football?
why: Question order: How long + have + subject + been + -ing?
questions.tip: Clue words: for / since / How long? / all day → have been + -ing. How many? / a number / finished result → have + V3.

questions.q: True or false: "He has been writing five letters" is the best way to say that he finished five letters.

similar.q: Which is correct for a finished result: "I have read / have been reading two books this week"?

why: False. A number of finished things (*five letters*) is a result → present perfect: *He has written five letters.*
*has been writing* tells us about the activity and how long, not how many.
questions.tip: Clue words: for / since / How long? / all day → have been + -ing. How many? / a number / finished result → have + V3.
